headings.title: Introduction to Skilled Nursing Facilities
headings.content: A **Skilled Nursing Facility (SNF)** is a specialized health care setting that provides round-the-clock medical care and rehabilitation services. Unlike basic assisted living communities, which primarily help with daily personal tasks, SNFs are staffed by licensed healthcare professionals capable of handling complex medical needs. Patients typically arrive here after being discharged from an acute care hospital but still require clinical oversight before returning home. Common reasons for admission include post-surgical recovery, severe stroke management, long-term intravenous therapy, and advanced wound care.

headings.title: Services and Levels of Care Provided
headings.content:
Care within a skilled nursing facility is divided into short-term rehabilitation and long-term custodial support. Short-term residents focus on regaining independence after an acute illness, injury, or surgery. Long-term residents suffer from chronic, progressive conditions requiring permanent nursing assistance.

- **Skilled Nursing Care**: Medication administration, wound care, catheter management, and vital sign monitoring performed by nurses.
- **Rehabilitative Therapies**: Physical, occupational, and speech therapy aimed at restoring functional capacity.
- **Custodial Support**: Assistance with activities of daily living such as bathing, dressing, and feeding for individuals unable to care for themselves.

headings.title: Admission Criteria and Patient Eligibility
headings.content: Admission to a skilled nursing facility requires meeting specific clinical and administrative criteria. Generally, a patient must have a qualifying hospital stay of at least three consecutive days for Medicare coverage to apply. The individual must also demonstrate a daily need for skilled nursing or therapy services that cannot be safely managed at home or in a lower level of care. A physician must order the placement and certify that the patient's medical condition warrants professional facility-based supervision.

headings.title: The Role of the Nursing Team in SNFs
headings.content: The nursing team forms the backbone of daily operations in a skilled nursing facility. Registered Nurses (RNs) coordinate care plans, assess complex clinical changes, and supervise licensed practical nurses and nursing assistants. Licensed Practical Nurses (LPNs) administer medications, change dressings, and monitor routine clinical parameters. Nursing Assistants (CNAs) handle frontline patient care, reporting changes in skin integrity, mood, or intake directly to the licensed staff. Team communication is essential to catch subtle signs of decline early.

headings.title: Interdisciplinary Healthcare Collaboration
headings.content: Optimal resident outcomes rely on close teamwork among diverse healthcare professionals. Nurses collaborate daily with physical therapists, occupational therapists, speech-language pathologists, social workers, dietitians, and attending physicians. For instance, a speech therapist evaluates swallowing difficulties while the nurse ensures safe administration of crushed medications with food. Regular care conferences bring these disciplines together with the patient and family to evaluate progress and update recovery goals.

headings.title: Patient Assessment, Care Planning, and Documentation
headings.content: Thorough documentation and standardized assessment tools drive clinical decision-making in SNFs. The **Minimum Data Set (MDS)** is a federally mandated assessment tool completed upon admission and periodically thereafter to track health status across multiple domains. Nurses use MDS findings to create individualized care plans that address specific deficits. Accurate charting ensures continuity of care across shifts, meets legal requirements, and secures appropriate reimbursement for services rendered.

headings.title: Rehabilitation and Restorative Nursing Care
headings.content: Restorative nursing bridges the gap between formal therapy sessions and everyday living. While physical and occupational therapists design specific recovery programs, nurses and care assistants reinforce these practices during routine daily care. Restorative programs prevent functional decline by encouraging residents to perform tasks independently, such as feeding themselves or walking to the dining room. Maintaining mobility reduces complications like pressure ulcers, contractures, and deep vein thrombosis.

headings.title: Regulations, Quality Standards, and Safety
headings.content: Skilled nursing facilities operate under strict government regulations to protect vulnerable residents. State and federal agencies conduct regular inspections to evaluate infection control, medication safety, resident rights, and environmental conditions. Facilities must track quality indicators such as fall rates, pressure ulcer development, and weight loss. Maintaining compliance requires continuous staff training, rigorous incident reporting, and prompt correction of any identified safety hazards.

headings.title: Transition of Care and Discharge Planning
headings.content: Discharge planning begins on the day of admission to ensure a smooth transition back to the community or a lower level of care. The interdisciplinary team assesses the patient's home environment, equipment needs, and family caregiver readiness. Nurses provide comprehensive education on medication regimens, wound care, and warning signs that require medical attention. Coordinating outpatient therapy and follow-up physician appointments minimizes the risk of preventable hospital readmissions.
